quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Components, JSX, and Props
quizzes.intro: Check whether you understand React’s declarative model, JSX basics, and props before state and effects.

questions.prompt: What does “UI as a function of state” emphasize in React?

options.text: You manually patch DOM nodes for every tiny change as the primary style
You describe what the UI should look like for current data, and React updates the view to match
State is illegal in React components
React only works without JavaScript

questions.explanation: React’s declarative model focuses on rendering UI from current state and props rather than hand-updating the DOM everywhere.

wrongExplanations.a: That describes classic imperative DOM scripting more than React’s core style.
wrongExplanations.c: State is central to interactive React UIs.
wrongExplanations.d: React is a JavaScript library for building UIs.

questions.prompt: Which JSX attribute correctly replaces the HTML class attribute?

options.text: class
className
cssClass
classnameProp

questions.explanation: In JSX, className maps to the DOM class attribute because class is a reserved word in JavaScript.

wrongExplanations.a: class is invalid/confusing in JSX compared with className.
wrongExplanations.c: cssClass is not the standard React JSX attribute.
wrongExplanations.d: classnameProp is not the React convention.

questions.prompt: How should a child component treat props?

options.text: As read-only inputs from the parent that should not be mutated
As writable globals shared by every component automatically
As CSS-only values that cannot hold text
As a replacement for JavaScript functions

questions.explanation: Props flow down and should be treated as immutable inputs for predictable data flow.

wrongExplanations.b: Props are not automatic writable globals.
wrongExplanations.c: Props can hold many value types, including text and objects.
wrongExplanations.d: Props pass data; they do not replace functions as a language feature.

questions.prompt: What is a React component in the essentials sense used here?

options.text: A database table
A function that returns a description of UI (React elements)
A CSS reset file
A server-only SQL query

questions.explanation: Function components receive props and return elements describing the UI.

wrongExplanations.a: Databases are outside the component definition.
wrongExplanations.c: CSS resets are styling concerns, not components.
wrongExplanations.d: SQL queries are data-layer concerns, not React components.

questions.prompt: Why is composition with children often useful?

options.text: Because it forces every component to fetch from an API
Because a wrapper can provide structure without hard-coding its inner content
Because children disable props permanently
Because React forbids nesting components otherwise

questions.explanation: Passing children lets layout/wrapper components remain flexible about what they contain.

wrongExplanations.d: Nesting components is normal and allowed.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — State, Lists, and Forms
quizzes.intro: Test state updates, keys, controlled inputs, and lifting state.

options.text: A CSS stylesheet injector only
A state value and a setter that schedules a re-render with updated state
A direct mutable reference that React never re-reads
A replacement for HTML forms in the browser chrome

questions.explanation: useState returns current state and a setter used to update UI over time.

wrongExplanations.a: useState is about component state, not injecting stylesheets.
wrongExplanations.c: You should update through the setter rather than silent mutation.
wrongExplanations.d: Forms still use input elements; React state can control them.

questions.prompt: Why avoid mutating arrays in state directly?

options.text: Because React relies on updating state with new values/references to track changes reliably
Because arrays are illegal in React
Because mutation automatically deletes the component
Because keys become CSS classes when you mutate

questions.explanation: Immutable updates (new arrays/objects) help React detect changes and keep UI in sync.

wrongExplanations.b: Arrays are commonly stored in state.
wrongExplanations.c: Mutation does not delete components; it risks stale UI.
wrongExplanations.d: Keys and CSS classes are separate concepts.

questions.prompt: What should a list key usually represent?

options.text: A stable unique identity for each item, ideally from your data
A random value regenerated every render on purpose
The component author’s first name
The current mouse x-coordinate

questions.explanation: Stable unique keys help React reconcile list updates correctly.

wrongExplanations.b: Random keys every render defeat the purpose and cause remount churn.
wrongExplanations.c: Author names are not item identities.
wrongExplanations.d: Pointer position is unrelated to list identity.

questions.prompt: What makes an input controlled in React?

options.text: Its value is driven by React state and updated via onChange
It has no value attribute and never fires events
It is styled with inline CSS only
It must be an uncontrolled file input forever

questions.explanation: Controlled inputs use state as the source of truth for the displayed value.

wrongExplanations.b: That would not be an interactive controlled field.
wrongExplanations.c: Styling does not define controlled behavior.
wrongExplanations.d: File inputs have special cases; the definition of controlled is broader.

questions.prompt: When should you lift state up?

options.text: Whenever any component exists, always to the absolute root without thought
When multiple children need to share and synchronize the same changing data
Never; duplicated sibling state is always better
Only for CSS hover effects

questions.explanation: Shared interactive data belongs in the closest common parent to keep one source of truth.

wrongExplanations.a: Lifting everything to the root creates unnecessary coupling.
wrongExplanations.c: Duplicated state often drifts out of sync.
wrongExplanations.d: Hover styling is not the main reason to lift React state.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Effects, Hooks, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Apply essentials to side effects, hook rules, and debugging judgment.

questions.prompt: What belongs in useEffect rather than during pure render?

options.text: Calculating a filtered list from props already in memory
Fetching data, subscriptions, or other side effects that talk to the outside world
Returning JSX
Declaring a const for a derived boolean

questions.explanation: Effects synchronize with external systems; pure calculations should usually happen during render.

wrongExplanations.a: Derived filtering is typically computed while rendering.
wrongExplanations.c: Returning JSX is the component’s render job.
wrongExplanations.d: Derived booleans are normally computed in render.

questions.prompt: Why include values like slug in an effect dependency array when the effect uses them?

options.text: So the effect re-runs when those reactive inputs change and stays consistent
Because dependency arrays are only decorative comments
To prevent JavaScript from parsing the file
Because React forbids fetch outside dependency arrays forever

questions.explanation: Dependencies tell React when to re-run the effect so it uses current values.

wrongExplanations.c: They do not affect parsing that way.
wrongExplanations.d: Fetching can also happen in event handlers; dependencies are about effect correctness.

questions.prompt: Which hook usage violates the Rules of Hooks?

options.text: Calling useState at the top level of a function component
Calling useState inside a condition so it sometimes does not run
Calling useEffect at the top level with a cleanup function
Calling a custom hook unconditionally from a component

questions.explanation: Hooks must be called in the same order every render; conditional calls break that rule.

wrongExplanations.c: Top-level useEffect with cleanup is normal.

questions.prompt: What is a common reason to use a cancelled flag in a fetch effect?

options.text: To style buttons with CSS modules
To avoid applying stale responses or setting state after the request is no longer relevant
To disable JSX permanently
To convert props into CSS variables automatically

questions.explanation: Cleanup can mark work cancelled so late responses do not update the wrong UI state.

wrongExplanations.a: Styling is unrelated to fetch cancellation flags.
wrongExplanations.d: Props-to-CSS conversion is not what cancelled flags do.

questions.prompt: Why is storing a value that can be computed from existing state often a mistake?

options.text: Because derived values are illegal in JavaScript
Because mirrored state can drift out of sync; computing during render stays honest
Because React cannot display computed strings
Because useState only accepts objects

questions.explanation: Extra synchronized state creates opportunities for inconsistency; derive when possible.

wrongExplanations.c: React can render computed strings easily.
wrongExplanations.d: useState accepts many value types, including primitives.

questions.prompt: A button’s handler looks like onClick={handleSave()}. What is the likely problem?

options.text: Nothing—this always waits for the click before calling
handleSave runs during render, and onClick receives its return value instead of a click handler function
React will convert it into a CSS animation
It disables all hooks in the tree

questions.explanation: Including parentheses calls the function immediately during render unless you wrap it intentionally.

wrongExplanations.a: The call happens at render time, not on click.
wrongExplanations.c: Event props are not CSS animations.
wrongExplanations.d: This mistake does not disable the Rules of Hooks system-wide.
